newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota 'hybrid' car breaks new ground -- analysts.
newsitem.headline: Toyota 'hybrid' car breaks new ground -- analysts.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp's plan to mass produce "hybrid" multi-fuelled vehicles later this year marks a big step in automakers' efforts to go mainstream with alternative engines, analysts say.

The company announced on Monday that its new Hybrid System vehicles -- which group a gasoline engine, an electric generator and an electric motor under the same hood -- will hit the road by the end of this year.

"While this is one of the more conventional units, as it still houses a gasoline engine, the production levels we're talking about make it one of the most solid attempts by an automaker to venture into the mainstream with an alternative engine," said Peter Boardman, a Tokyo-based auto analyst with UBS Securities.
A new assembly line for the hybrid vehicle, to be built at Toyota's plant in central Japan's Aichi prefecture, will produce some 1,000 vehicles per month, a company spokesman said.

"This is going to be a mass-produced vehicle," the spokesman told Reuters. "Certainly not on the scale of our Corona model, which we produce at levels of tens of thousands per month, but probably on the scale of 1,000 per month." he added.

In addition to delivering fuel efficiency of almost 80 miles (125 km) per gallon, the system cuts carbon dioxide emissions by more than half and emissions of carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxide by as much as 90 percent, Toyota said.
But analysts say production volumes, price, and the marketing effort involved, more than the technology itself, mark the biggest strides for Toyota.
"Toyota has a wide-ranging inventory of different emissions-reducing...engines it is developing," Boardman said.

Toyota has a long list of innovative engines to its credit, including a lean-burn engine in 1984 and a direct injection gasoline engine in 1996, but analysts say the company's many breakthroughs have not always translated into higher profits.
Toyota says the car will be affordable as well.

"We're pricing it so that it won't be more than 500,000 yen more than customers would pay for an equivalent conventional vehicle," a Toyota spokesman said. That, more than anything, analysts said, gives the car a fighting chance.
"The most meaningful stride taken by Toyota in this initiative is to make the car affordable," said Merrill Lynch auto analyst Takaki Nakanishi.
"The first step for the success of any of these vehicles will be to make them an economical alternative for the average driver," he added.
Nissan Motor Co Ltd said in May it had developed a hybrid gasoline-electric vehicle it hoped to market by the end of 1998.
